It is one of the shrines claiming to be the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of former [[Bungo Province]]. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on April 15.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Sasamuta Jinja is {{nihongo|'''Sasamuta-Ōkami'''|西寒多大神|}}, which is an amalgamation of: * {{nihongo|'''[[Amaterasu]]'''|天照皇大御神|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto]]'''|月読尊|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Ame-no-oshihomimi]]'''|天忍穗耳尊|}} ==History== According to the ''Ōita Gunshi'' (大分郡志), [[Empress Jingu]] visited Mount Sasamuta on her way back from the conquest of the [[Korean Peninsula]], and planted a white flag at the top of the mountain as proof of her visit. The local people revered it and tied a fence around it to worship it. Later, in April of the 9th year of [[Emperor Ojin]]'s reign, [[Takenouchi no Sukune]] built a shrine on the site, which established that the mountain was a [[sacred mountain]]. The shrine first appears in documentary history in an article dated March 22, 869, in the ''[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]'', where it is written that Sasamuta-Ōkami was given the rank of Junior Fifth Rank. It reappears in the ''[[Engishiki]]'' listing of the mid-[[Heian period]], where it has the distinction of being classed as the only "major shrine" in Bungo Province. Although it declined after the late Heian period, it was revived by the [[Ōtomo clan]], from the [[Kamakura period]] onwards. In March 1408, Ōtomo Shinze relocated the shrine from the top of the mountain to its current location at the foot of the mountain. During the [[Edo period]], the [[Makino clan]] and then the [[Naitō clan]] of [[Nobeoka Domain]], frequently sponsored renovation and repairs, and their feudal retainers also donated items such as [[tōro|stone lanterns]].{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} During the [[Meiji period]] era of [[State Shinto]], the shrine was designated as a {{nihongo|National shrine, 2nd rank |国幣中社|[[kokuhei-chūsha]]}} under the [[Modern system of ranked Shinto Shrines]]Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' pp. 125. {{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} ==Mannen-bashi== The {{nihongo|Mannenbashi|万年橋||}} is a 22-meter long single-arch stone bridge that spans the Samuda River (commonly known as the Misogi River), which flows through the entrance to Sasamuta Shrine. It was designated as a Tangible Cultural Property of Ōita Prefecture on April 8, 1980. Not only is the main structure an arch, but the road surface also forms a gentle arc, and the stonework between the road surface and the arch is narrow. In 1862 at the end of the Edo period, the village headman of Samuta village, which was then part of the [[Nobeoka Domain]], started a stone masonry business in Shibakita village, Ono district (currently [[Bungo-ono, Ōita]]), which was part of [[Oka Domain]]. ==Gallery== Sasamuta-jinja torii.JPG|Torii Hongusan.JPG|Mout Hongu Sasamuta-jinja honden.JPG|Honden Sasamuta-jinja kaguraden.JPG|Kagura-den Sasamuta-jinja Mannen-bashi.JPG|Mannen-bashi (P.ICIP) ==See also== *[[List of Shinto shrines]] *[[Ichinomiya]] ==References== * Plutschow, Herbe. The shrine first appears in documentary history in an article dated March 22, 869, in the ''[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]'', where it is written that Sasamuta-Ōkami was given the rank of Junior Fifth Rank. It reappears in the ''[[Engishiki]]'' listing of the mid-[[Heian period]], where it has the distinction of being classed as the only "major shrine" in Bungo Province. Although it declined after the late Heian period, it was revived by the [[Ōtomo clan]], from the [[Kamakura period]] onwards. In March 1408, Ōtomo Shinze relocated the shrine from the top of the mountain to its current location at the foot of the mountain. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' pp. 125. {{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} ==Mannen-bashi== The {{nihongo|Mannenbashi|万年橋||}} is a 22-meter long single-arch stone bridge that spans the Samuda River (commonly known as the Misogi River), which flows through the entrance to Sasamuta Shrine. The local people revered it and tied a fence around it to worship it. Later, in April of the 9th year of [[Emperor Ojin]]'s reign, [[Takenouchi no Sukune]] built a shrine on the site, which established that the mountain was a [[sacred mountain]]. Although it declined after the late Heian period, it was revived by the [[Ōtomo clan]], from the [[Kamakura period]] onwards. In March 1408, Ōtomo Shinze relocated the shrine from the top of the mountain to its current location at the foot of the mountain. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' pp. 125. {{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} ==Mannen-bashi== The {{nihongo|Mannenbashi|万年橋||}} is a 22-meter long single-arch stone bridge that spans the Samuda River (commonly known as the Misogi River), which flows through the entrance to Sasamuta Shrine. {{Short description|Shinto shrine in Ōita Prefecture, Japan}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Sasamuta Jinja
西寒多神社 | image = Sasamuta-jinja haiden-2.JPG | caption = Haiden of Sasamuta Jinja {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Oita Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|33|10|22|N|131|35|54.2|E|region:JP-35|display=inline,title}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = | deity = Sasamuta-Ōkami | founded_by = | established = unknown | date_destroyed = | location = 1644 Soda, Ōita-shi, Ōita-ken | website = | architecture_style = | festival =April 15 | leadership = | footnotes = }} {{nihongo|'''Sasamuta Jinja'''|西寒多神社}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in the Soda neighborhood of the city of [[Ōita, Ōita | Ōita]] in [[Ōita Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is one of the shrines claiming to be the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of former [[Bungo Province]]. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on April 15.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Sasamuta Jinja is {{nihongo|'''Sasamuta-Ōkami'''|西寒多大神|}}, which is an amalgamation of: * {{nihongo|'''[[Amaterasu]]'''|天照皇大御神|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto]]'''|月読尊|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Ame-no-oshihomimi]]'''|天忍穗耳尊|}} ==History== According to the ''Ōita Gunshi'' (大分郡志), [[Empress Jingu]] visited Mount Sasamuta on her way back from the conquest of the [[Korean Peninsula]], and planted a white flag at the top of the mountain as proof of her visit. The local people revered it and tied a fence around it to worship it. Later, in April of the 9th year of [[Emperor Ojin]]'s reign, [[Takenouchi no Sukune]] built a shrine on the site, which established that the mountain was a [[sacred mountain]]. The shrine first appears in documentary history in an article dated March 22, 869, in the ''[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]'', where it is written that Sasamuta-Ōkami was given the rank of Junior Fifth Rank. It reappears in the ''[[Engishiki]]'' listing of the mid-[[Heian period]], where it has the distinction of being classed as the only "major shrine" in Bungo Province. Although it declined after the late Heian period, it was revived by the [[Ōtomo clan]], from the [[Kamakura period]] onwards. In March 1408, Ōtomo Shinze relocated the shrine from the top of the mountain to its current location at the foot of the mountain. During the [[Edo period]], the [[Makino clan]] and then the [[Naitō clan]] of [[Nobeoka Domain]], frequently sponsored renovation and repairs, and their feudal retainers also donated items such as [[tōro|stone lanterns]].{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} During the [[Meiji period]] era of [[State Shinto]], the shrine was designated as a {{nihongo|National shrine, 2nd rank |国幣中社|[[kokuhei-chūsha]]}} under the [[Modern system of ranked Shinto Shrines]]Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' pp. 125. {{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} ==Mannen-bashi== The {{nihongo|Mannenbashi|万年橋||}} is a 22-meter long single-arch stone bridge that spans the Samuda River (commonly known as the Misogi River), which flows through the entrance to Sasamuta Shrine. It was designated as a Tangible Cultural Property of Ōita Prefecture on April 8, 1980. Not only is the main structure an arch, but the road surface also forms a gentle arc, and the stonework between the road surface and the arch is narrow. In 1862 at the end of the Edo period, the village headman of Samuta village, which was then part of the [[Nobeoka Domain]], started a stone masonry business in Shibakita village, Ono district (currently [[Bungo-ono, Ōita]]), which was part of [[Oka Domain]]. ==Gallery== Sasamuta-jinja torii.JPG|Torii Hongusan.JPG|Mout Hongu Sasamuta-jinja honden.JPG|Honden Sasamuta-jinja kaguraden.JPG|Kagura-den Sasamuta-jinja Mannen-bashi.JPG|Mannen-bashi (P.ICIP) ==See also== *[[List of Shinto shrines]] *[[Ichinomiya]] ==References== * Plutschow, Herbe. ''Matsuri: The Festivals of Japan''. RoutledgeCurzon (1996) {{ISBN|1-873410-63-8}} * [[Richard Ponsonby-Fane|Ponsonby-Fane]], Richard Arthur Brabazon. (1959). [https://books.google.com/books?id=SLAeAAAAMAAJ&q=The+Imperial+House+of+Japan ''The Imperial House of Japan.''] Kyoto: Ponsonby Memorial Society. {{Short description|Shinto shrine in Ōita Prefecture, Japan}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Sasamuta Jinja
西寒多神社 | image = Sasamuta-jinja haiden-2.JPG | caption = Haiden of Sasamuta Jinja {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Oita Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|33|10|22|N|131|35|54.2|E|region:JP-35|display=inline,title}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = | deity = Sasamuta-Ōkami | founded_by = | established = unknown | date_destroyed = | location = 1644 Soda, Ōita-shi, Ōita-ken | website = | architecture_style = | festival =April 15 | leadership = | footnotes = }} {{nihongo|'''Sasamuta Jinja'''|西寒多神社}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in the Soda neighborhood of the city of [[Ōita, Ōita | Ōita]] in [[Ōita Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is one of the shrines claiming to be the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of former [[Bungo Province]]. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on April 15.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Sasamuta Jinja is {{nihongo|'''Sasamuta-Ōkami'''|西寒多大神|}}, which is an amalgamation of: * {{nihongo|'''[[Amaterasu]]'''|天照皇大御神|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto]]'''|月読尊|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Ame-no-oshihomimi]]'''|天忍穗耳尊|}} ==History== According to the ''Ōita Gunshi'' (大分郡志), [[Empress Jingu]] visited Mount Sasamuta on her way back from the conquest of the [[Korean Peninsula]], and planted a white flag at the top of the mountain as proof of her visit. The local people revered it and tied a fence around it to worship it. Later, in April of the 9th year of [[Emperor Ojin]]'s reign, [[Takenouchi no Sukune]] built a shrine on the site, which established that the mountain was a [[sacred mountain]]. The shrine first appears in documentary history in an article dated March 22, 869, in the ''[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]'', where it is written that Sasamuta-Ōkami was given the rank of Junior Fifth Rank. It reappears in the ''[[Engishiki]]'' listing of the mid-[[Heian period]], where it has the distinction of being classed as the only "major shrine" in Bungo Province. Although it declined after the late Heian period, it was revived by the [[Ōtomo clan]], from the [[Kamakura period]] onwards. In March 1408, Ōtomo Shinze relocated the shrine from the top of the mountain to its current location at the foot of the mountain. During the [[Edo period]], the [[Makino clan]] and then the [[Naitō clan]] of [[Nobeoka Domain]], frequently sponsored renovation and repairs, and their feudal retainers also donated items such as [[tōro|stone lanterns]].{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} During the [[Meiji period]] era of [[State Shinto]], the shrine was designated as a {{nihongo|National shrine, 2nd rank |国幣中社|[[kokuhei-chūsha]]}} under the [[Modern system of ranked Shinto Shrines]]Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' pp. 125. {{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} ==Mannen-bashi== The {{nihongo|Mannenbashi|万年橋||}} is a 22-meter long single-arch stone bridge that spans the Samuda River (commonly known as the Misogi River), which flows through the entrance to Sasamuta Shrine. It was designated as a Tangible Cultural Property of Ōita Prefecture on April 8, 1980. Not only is the main structure an arch, but the road surface also forms a gentle arc, and the stonework between the road surface and the arch is narrow. In 1862 at the end of the Edo period, the village headman of Samuta village, which was then part of the [[Nobeoka Domain]], started a stone masonry business in Shibakita village, Ono district (currently [[Bungo-ono, Ōita]]), which was part of [[Oka Domain]]. ==Gallery== Sasamuta-jinja torii.JPG|Torii Hongusan.JPG|Mout Hongu Sasamuta-jinja honden.JPG|Honden Sasamuta-jinja kaguraden.JPG|Kagura-den Sasamuta-jinja Mannen-bashi.JPG|Mannen-bashi (P.ICIP) ==See also== *[[List of Shinto shrines]] *[[Ichinomiya]] ==References== * Plutschow, Herbe. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on April 15.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Sasamuta Jinja is {{nihongo|'''Sasamuta-Ōkami'''|西寒多大神|}}, which is an amalgamation of: * {{nihongo|'''[[Amaterasu]]'''|天照皇大御神|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto]]'''|月読尊|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Ame-no-oshihomimi]]'''|天忍穗耳尊|}} ==History== According to the ''Ōita Gunshi'' (大分郡志), [[Empress Jingu]] visited Mount Sasamuta on her way back from the conquest of the [[Korean Peninsula]], and planted a white flag at the top of the mountain as proof of her visit. The local people revered it and tied a fence around it to worship it. Later, in April of the 9th year of [[Emperor Ojin]]'s reign, [[Takenouchi no Sukune]] built a shrine on the site, which established that the mountain was a [[sacred mountain]]. The shrine first appears in documentary history in an article dated March 22, 869, in the ''[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]'', where it is written that Sasamuta-Ōkami was given the rank of Junior Fifth Rank. It reappears in the ''[[Engishiki]]'' listing of the mid-[[Heian period]], where it has the distinction of being classed as the only "major shrine" in Bungo Province. Although it declined after the late Heian period, it was revived by the [[Ōtomo clan]], from the [[Kamakura period]] onwards. In March 1408, Ōtomo Shinze relocated the shrine from the top of the mountain to its current location at the foot of the mountain. During the [[Edo period]], the [[Makino clan]] and then the [[Naitō clan]] of [[Nobeoka Domain]], frequently sponsored renovation and repairs, and their feudal retainers also donated items such as [[tōro|stone lanterns]].{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} During the [[Meiji period]] era of [[State Shinto]], the shrine was designated as a {{nihongo|National shrine, 2nd rank |国幣中社|[[kokuhei-chūsha]]}} under the [[Modern system of ranked Shinto Shrines]]Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' pp. 125. {{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} ==Mannen-bashi== The {{nihongo|Mannenbashi|万年橋||}} is a 22-meter long single-arch stone bridge that spans the Samuda River (commonly known as the Misogi River), which flows through the entrance to Sasamuta Shrine. It was designated as a Tangible Cultural Property of Ōita Prefecture on April 8, 1980. Not only is the main structure an arch, but the road surface also forms a gentle arc, and the stonework between the road surface and the arch is narrow. In 1862 at the end of the Edo period, the village headman of Samuta village, which was then part of the [[Nobeoka Domain]], started a stone masonry business in Shibakita village, Ono district (currently [[Bungo-ono, Ōita]]), which was part of [[Oka Domain]]. ==Gallery== Sasamuta-jinja torii.JPG|Torii Hongusan.JPG|Mout Hongu Sasamuta-jinja honden.JPG|Honden Sasamuta-jinja kaguraden.JPG|Kagura-den Sasamuta-jinja Mannen-bashi.JPG|Mannen-bashi (P.ICIP) ==See also== *[[List of Shinto shrines]] *[[Ichinomiya]] ==References== * Plutschow, Herbe. {{Short description|Shinto shrine in Ōita Prefecture, Japan}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Sasamuta Jinja
西寒多神社 | image = Sasamuta-jinja haiden-2.JPG | caption = Haiden of Sasamuta Jinja {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Oita Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|33|10|22|N|131|35|54.2|E|region:JP-35|display=inline,title}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = | deity = Sasamuta-Ōkami | founded_by = | established = unknown | date_destroyed = | location = 1644 Soda, Ōita-shi, Ōita-ken | website = | architecture_style = | festival =April 15 | leadership = | footnotes = }} {{nihongo|'''Sasamuta Jinja'''|西寒多神社}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in the Soda neighborhood of the city of [[Ōita, Ōita | Ōita]] in [[Ōita Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is one of the shrines claiming to be the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of former [[Bungo Province]]. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on April 15.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Sasamuta Jinja is {{nihongo|'''Sasamuta-Ōkami'''|西寒多大神|}}, which is an amalgamation of: * {{nihongo|'''[[Amaterasu]]'''|天照皇大御神|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto]]'''|月読尊|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Ame-no-oshihomimi]]'''|天忍穗耳尊|}} ==History== According to the ''Ōita Gunshi'' (大分郡志), [[Empress Jingu]] visited Mount Sasamuta on her way back from the conquest of the [[Korean Peninsula]], and planted a white flag at the top of the mountain as proof of her visit. The local people revered it and tied a fence around it to worship it. Later, in April of the 9th year of [[Emperor Ojin]]'s reign, [[Takenouchi no Sukune]] built a shrine on the site, which established that the mountain was a [[sacred mountain]]. The shrine first appears in documentary history in an article dated March 22, 869, in the ''[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]'', where it is written that Sasamuta-Ōkami was given the rank of Junior Fifth Rank. It reappears in the ''[[Engishiki]]'' listing of the mid-[[Heian period]], where it has the distinction of being classed as the only "major shrine" in Bungo Province. Although it declined after the late Heian period, it was revived by the [[Ōtomo clan]], from the [[Kamakura period]] onwards. In March 1408, Ōtomo Shinze relocated the shrine from the top of the mountain to its current location at the foot of the mountain. During the [[Edo period]], the [[Makino clan]] and then the [[Naitō clan]] of [[Nobeoka Domain]], frequently sponsored renovation and repairs, and their feudal retainers also donated items such as [[tōro|stone lanterns]].{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} During the [[Meiji period]] era of [[State Shinto]], the shrine was designated as a {{nihongo|National shrine, 2nd rank |国幣中社|[[kokuhei-chūsha]]}} under the [[Modern system of ranked Shinto Shrines]]Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' pp. 125. {{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} ==Mannen-bashi== The {{nihongo|Mannenbashi|万年橋||}} is a 22-meter long single-arch stone bridge that spans the Samuda River (commonly known as the Misogi River), which flows through the entrance to Sasamuta Shrine. It was designated as a Tangible Cultural Property of Ōita Prefecture on April 8, 1980. Not only is the main structure an arch, but the road surface also forms a gentle arc, and the stonework between the road surface and the arch is narrow. In 1862 at the end of the Edo period, the village headman of Samuta village, which was then part of the [[Nobeoka Domain]], started a stone masonry business in Shibakita village, Ono district (currently [[Bungo-ono, Ōita]]), which was part of [[Oka Domain]]. ==Gallery== Sasamuta-jinja torii.JPG|Torii Hongusan.JPG|Mout Hongu Sasamuta-jinja honden.JPG|Honden Sasamuta-jinja kaguraden.JPG|Kagura-den Sasamuta-jinja Mannen-bashi.JPG|Mannen-bashi (P.ICIP) ==See also== *[[List of Shinto shrines]] *[[Ichinomiya]] ==References== * Plutschow, Herbe. {{Short description|Shinto shrine in Ōita Prefecture, Japan}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Sasamuta Jinja
西寒多神社 | image = Sasamuta-jinja haiden-2.JPG | caption = Haiden of Sasamuta Jinja {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Oita Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|33|10|22|N|131|35|54.2|E|region:JP-35|display=inline,title}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = | deity = Sasamuta-Ōkami | founded_by = | established = unknown | date_destroyed = | location = 1644 Soda, Ōita-shi, Ōita-ken | website = | architecture_style = | festival =April 15 | leadership = | footnotes = }} {{nihongo|'''Sasamuta Jinja'''|西寒多神社}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in the Soda neighborhood of the city of [[Ōita, Ōita | Ōita]] in [[Ōita Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is one of the shrines claiming to be the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of former [[Bungo Province]]. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on April 15.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Sasamuta Jinja is {{nihongo|'''Sasamuta-Ōkami'''|西寒多大神|}}, which is an amalgamation of: * {{nihongo|'''[[Amaterasu]]'''|天照皇大御神|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto]]'''|月読尊|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Ame-no-oshihomimi]]'''|天忍穗耳尊|}} ==History== According to the ''Ōita Gunshi'' (大分郡志), [[Empress Jingu]] visited Mount Sasamuta on her way back from the conquest of the [[Korean Peninsula]], and planted a white flag at the top of the mountain as proof of her visit. The local people revered it and tied a fence around it to worship it. Later, in April of the 9th year of [[Emperor Ojin]]'s reign, [[Takenouchi no Sukune]] built a shrine on the site, which established that the mountain was a [[sacred mountain]]. The shrine first appears in documentary history in an article dated March 22, 869, in the ''[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]'', where it is written that Sasamuta-Ōkami was given the rank of Junior Fifth Rank. It reappears in the ''[[Engishiki]]'' listing of the mid-[[Heian period]], where it has the distinction of being classed as the only "major shrine" in Bungo Province. Although it declined after the late Heian period, it was revived by the [[Ōtomo clan]], from the [[Kamakura period]] onwards. In March 1408, Ōtomo Shinze relocated the shrine from the top of the mountain to its current location at the foot of the mountain. During the [[Edo period]], the [[Makino clan]] and then the [[Naitō clan]] of [[Nobeoka Domain]], frequently sponsored renovation and repairs, and their feudal retainers also donated items such as [[tōro|stone lanterns]].{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} During the [[Meiji period]] era of [[State Shinto]], the shrine was designated as a {{nihongo|National shrine, 2nd rank |国幣中社|[[kokuhei-chūsha]]}} under the [[Modern system of ranked Shinto Shrines]]Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' pp. 125. {{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} ==Mannen-bashi== The {{nihongo|Mannenbashi|万年橋||}} is a 22-meter long single-arch stone bridge that spans the Samuda River (commonly known as the Misogi River), which flows through the entrance to Sasamuta Shrine. It was designated as a Tangible Cultural Property of Ōita Prefecture on April 8, 1980. Not only is the main structure an arch, but the road surface also forms a gentle arc, and the stonework between the road surface and the arch is narrow. In 1862 at the end of the Edo period, the village headman of Samuta village, which was then part of the [[Nobeoka Domain]], started a stone masonry business in Shibakita village, Ono district (currently [[Bungo-ono, Ōita]]), which was part of [[Oka Domain]]. ==Gallery== Sasamuta-jinja torii.JPG|Torii Hongusan.JPG|Mout Hongu Sasamuta-jinja honden.JPG|Honden Sasamuta-jinja kaguraden.JPG|Kagura-den Sasamuta-jinja Mannen-bashi.JPG|Mannen-bashi (P.ICIP) ==See also== *[[List of Shinto shrines]] *[[Ichinomiya]] ==References== * Plutschow, Herbe. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on April 15.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Sasamuta Jinja is {{nihongo|'''Sasamuta-Ōkami'''|西寒多大神|}}, which is an amalgamation of: * {{nihongo|'''[[Amaterasu]]'''|天照皇大御神|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto]]'''|月読尊|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Ame-no-oshihomimi]]'''|天忍穗耳尊|}} ==History== According to the ''Ōita Gunshi'' (大分郡志), [[Empress Jingu]] visited Mount Sasamuta on her way back from the conquest of the [[Korean Peninsula]], and planted a white flag at the top of the mountain as proof of her visit. The local people revered it and tied a fence around it to worship it. Later, in April of the 9th year of [[Emperor Ojin]]'s reign, [[Takenouchi no Sukune]] built a shrine on the site, which established that the mountain was a [[sacred mountain]]. The shrine first appears in documentary history in an article dated March 22, 869, in the ''[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]'', where it is written that Sasamuta-Ōkami was given the rank of Junior Fifth Rank. It reappears in the ''[[Engishiki]]'' listing of the mid-[[Heian period]], where it has the distinction of being classed as the only "major shrine" in Bungo Province. Although it declined after the late Heian period, it was revived by the [[Ōtomo clan]], from the [[Kamakura period]] onwards. In March 1408, Ōtomo Shinze relocated the shrine from the top of the mountain to its current location at the foot of the mountain. During the [[Edo period]], the [[Makino clan]] and then the [[Naitō clan]] of [[Nobeoka Domain]], frequently sponsored renovation and repairs, and their feudal retainers also donated items such as [[tōro|stone lanterns]].{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} During the [[Meiji period]] era of [[State Shinto]], the shrine was designated as a {{nihongo|National shrine, 2nd rank |国幣中社|[[kokuhei-chūsha]]}} under the [[Modern system of ranked Shinto Shrines]]Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' pp. 125. {{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} ==Mannen-bashi== The {{nihongo|Mannenbashi|万年橋||}} is a 22-meter long single-arch stone bridge that spans the Samuda River (commonly known as the Misogi River), which flows through the entrance to Sasamuta Shrine. It was designated as a Tangible Cultural Property of Ōita Prefecture on April 8, 1980. Not only is the main structure an arch, but the road surface also forms a gentle arc, and the stonework between the road surface and the arch is narrow. In 1862 at the end of the Edo period, the village headman of Samuta village, which was then part of the [[Nobeoka Domain]], started a stone masonry business in Shibakita village, Ono district (currently [[Bungo-ono, Ōita]]), which was part of [[Oka Domain]]. ==Gallery== Sasamuta-jinja torii.JPG|Torii Hongusan.JPG|Mout Hongu Sasamuta-jinja honden.JPG|Honden Sasamuta-jinja kaguraden.JPG|Kagura-den Sasamuta-jinja Mannen-bashi.JPG|Mannen-bashi (P.ICIP) ==See also== *[[List of Shinto shrines]] *[[Ichinomiya]] ==References== * Plutschow, Herbe. {{Short description|Shinto shrine in Ōita Prefecture, Japan}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Sasamuta Jinja
西寒多神社 | image = Sasamuta-jinja haiden-2.JPG | caption = Haiden of Sasamuta Jinja {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Oita Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|33|10|22|N|131|35|54.2|E|region:JP-35|display=inline,title}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = | deity = Sasamuta-Ōkami | founded_by = | established = unknown | date_destroyed = | location = 1644 Soda, Ōita-shi, Ōita-ken | website = | architecture_style = | festival =April 15 | leadership = | footnotes = }} {{nihongo|'''Sasamuta Jinja'''|西寒多神社}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in the Soda neighborhood of the city of [[Ōita, Ōita | Ōita]] in [[Ōita Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is one of the shrines claiming to be the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of former [[Bungo Province]]. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on April 15.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Sasamuta Jinja is {{nihongo|'''Sasamuta-Ōkami'''|西寒多大神|}}, which is an amalgamation of: * {{nihongo|'''[[Amaterasu]]'''|天照皇大御神|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto]]'''|月読尊|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Ame-no-oshihomimi]]'''|天忍穗耳尊|}} ==History== According to the ''Ōita Gunshi'' (大分郡志), [[Empress Jingu]] visited Mount Sasamuta on her way back from the conquest of the [[Korean Peninsula]], and planted a white flag at the top of the mountain as proof of her visit. The local people revered it and tied a fence around it to worship it. Later, in April of the 9th year of [[Emperor Ojin]]'s reign, [[Takenouchi no Sukune]] built a shrine on the site, which established that the mountain was a [[sacred mountain]]. The shrine first appears in documentary history in an article dated March 22, 869, in the ''[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]'', where it is written that Sasamuta-Ōkami was given the rank of Junior Fifth Rank. It reappears in the ''[[Engishiki]]'' listing of the mid-[[Heian period]], where it has the distinction of being classed as the only "major shrine" in Bungo Province. Although it declined after the late Heian period, it was revived by the [[Ōtomo clan]], from the [[Kamakura period]] onwards. In March 1408, Ōtomo Shinze relocated the shrine from the top of the mountain to its current location at the foot of the mountain. During the [[Edo period]], the [[Makino clan]] and then the [[Naitō clan]] of [[Nobeoka Domain]], frequently sponsored renovation and repairs, and their feudal retainers also donated items such as [[tōro|stone lanterns]].{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} During the [[Meiji period]] era of [[State Shinto]], the shrine was designated as a {{nihongo|National shrine, 2nd rank |国幣中社|[[kokuhei-chūsha]]}} under the [[Modern system of ranked Shinto Shrines]]Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' pp. 125. {{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} ==Mannen-bashi== The {{nihongo|Mannenbashi|万年橋||}} is a 22-meter long single-arch stone bridge that spans the Samuda River (commonly known as the Misogi River), which flows through the entrance to Sasamuta Shrine. It was designated as a Tangible Cultural Property of Ōita Prefecture on April 8, 1980. Not only is the main structure an arch, but the road surface also forms a gentle arc, and the stonework between the road surface and the arch is narrow. In 1862 at the end of the Edo period, the village headman of Samuta village, which was then part of the [[Nobeoka Domain]], started a stone masonry business in Shibakita village, Ono district (currently [[Bungo-ono, Ōita]]), which was part of [[Oka Domain]]. ==Gallery== Sasamuta-jinja torii.JPG|Torii Hongusan.JPG|Mout Hongu Sasamuta-jinja honden.JPG|Honden Sasamuta-jinja kaguraden.JPG|Kagura-den Sasamuta-jinja Mannen-bashi.JPG|Mannen-bashi (P.ICIP) ==See also== *[[List of Shinto shrines]] *[[Ichinomiya]] ==References== * Plutschow, Herbe. ''Matsuri: The Festivals of Japan''. RoutledgeCurzon (1996) {{ISBN|1-873410-63-8}} * [[Richard Ponsonby-Fane|Ponsonby-Fane]], Richard Arthur Brabazon. (1959). [https://books.google.com/books?id=SLAeAAAAMAAJ&q=The+Imperial+House+of+Japan ''The Imperial House of Japan.''] Kyoto: Ponsonby Memorial Society. 西寒多神社 | image = Sasamuta-jinja haiden-2.JPG | caption = Haiden of Sasamuta Jinja {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Oita Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|33|10|22|N|131|35|54.2|E|region:JP-35|display=inline,title}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = | deity = Sasamuta-Ōkami | founded_by = | established = unknown | date_destroyed = | location = 1644 Soda, Ōita-shi, Ōita-ken | website = | architecture_style = | festival =April 15 | leadership = | footnotes = }} {{nihongo|'''Sasamuta Jinja'''|西寒多神社}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in the Soda neighborhood of the city of [[Ōita, Ōita | Ōita]] in [[Ōita Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is one of the shrines claiming to be the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of former [[Bungo Province]]. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on April 15.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Sasamuta Jinja is {{nihongo|'''Sasamuta-Ōkami'''|西寒多大神|}}, which is an amalgamation of: * {{nihongo|'''[[Amaterasu]]'''|天照皇大御神|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto]]'''|月読尊|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Ame-no-oshihomimi]]'''|天忍穗耳尊|}} ==History== According to the ''Ōita Gunshi'' (大分郡志), [[Empress Jingu]] visited Mount Sasamuta on her way back from the conquest of the [[Korean Peninsula]], and planted a white flag at the top of the mountain as proof of her visit. The local people revered it and tied a fence around it to worship it. Later, in April of the 9th year of [[Emperor Ojin]]'s reign, [[Takenouchi no Sukune]] built a shrine on the site, which established that the mountain was a [[sacred mountain]]. The shrine first appears in documentary history in an article dated March 22, 869, in the ''[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]'', where it is written that Sasamuta-Ōkami was given the rank of Junior Fifth Rank. It reappears in the ''[[Engishiki]]'' listing of the mid-[[Heian period]], where it has the distinction of being classed as the only "major shrine" in Bungo Province. Although it declined after the late Heian period, it was revived by the [[Ōtomo clan]], from the [[Kamakura period]] onwards. In March 1408, Ōtomo Shinze relocated the shrine from the top of the mountain to its current location at the foot of the mountain. During the [[Edo period]], the [[Makino clan]] and then the [[Naitō clan]] of [[Nobeoka Domain]], frequently sponsored renovation and repairs, and their feudal retainers also donated items such as [[tōro|stone lanterns]].{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} During the [[Meiji period]] era of [[State Shinto]], the shrine was designated as a {{nihongo|National shrine, 2nd rank |国幣中社|[[kokuhei-chūsha]]}} under the [[Modern system of ranked Shinto Shrines]]Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' pp. 125. {{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} ==Mannen-bashi== The {{nihongo|Mannenbashi|万年橋||}} is a 22-meter long single-arch stone bridge that spans the Samuda River (commonly known as the Misogi River), which flows through the entrance to Sasamuta Shrine. It was designated as a Tangible Cultural Property of Ōita Prefecture on April 8, 1980. Not only is the main structure an arch, but the road surface also forms a gentle arc, and the stonework between the road surface and the arch is narrow. In 1862 at the end of the Edo period, the village headman of Samuta village, which was then part of the [[Nobeoka Domain]], started a stone masonry business in Shibakita village, Ono district (currently [[Bungo-ono, Ōita]]), which was part of [[Oka Domain]]. ==Gallery== Sasamuta-jinja torii.JPG|Torii Hongusan.JPG|Mout Hongu Sasamuta-jinja honden.JPG|Honden Sasamuta-jinja kaguraden.JPG|Kagura-den Sasamuta-jinja Mannen-bashi.JPG|Mannen-bashi (P.ICIP) ==See also== *[[List of Shinto shrines]] *[[Ichinomiya]] ==References== * Plutschow, Herbe. {{Short description|Shinto shrine in Ōita Prefecture, Japan}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Sasamuta Jinja
西寒多神社 | image = Sasamuta-jinja haiden-2.JPG | caption = Haiden of Sasamuta Jinja {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Oita Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|33|10|22|N|131|35|54.2|E|region:JP-35|display=inline,title}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = | deity = Sasamuta-Ōkami | founded_by = | established = unknown | date_destroyed = | location = 1644 Soda, Ōita-shi, Ōita-ken | website = | architecture_style = | festival =April 15 | leadership = | footnotes = }} {{nihongo|'''Sasamuta Jinja'''|西寒多神社}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in the Soda neighborhood of the city of [[Ōita, Ōita | Ōita]] in [[Ōita Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is one of the shrines claiming to be the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of former [[Bungo Province]]. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on April 15.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Sasamuta Jinja is {{nihongo|'''Sasamuta-Ōkami'''|西寒多大神|}}, which is an amalgamation of: * {{nihongo|'''[[Amaterasu]]'''|天照皇大御神|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto]]'''|月読尊|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Ame-no-oshihomimi]]'''|天忍穗耳尊|}} ==History== According to the ''Ōita Gunshi'' (大分郡志), [[Empress Jingu]] visited Mount Sasamuta on her way back from the conquest of the [[Korean Peninsula]], and planted a white flag at the top of the mountain as proof of her visit. The local people revered it and tied a fence around it to worship it. Later, in April of the 9th year of [[Emperor Ojin]]'s reign, [[Takenouchi no Sukune]] built a shrine on the site, which established that the mountain was a [[sacred mountain]]. The shrine first appears in documentary history in an article dated March 22, 869, in the ''[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]'', where it is written that Sasamuta-Ōkami was given the rank of Junior Fifth Rank. It reappears in the ''[[Engishiki]]'' listing of the mid-[[Heian period]], where it has the distinction of being classed as the only "major shrine" in Bungo Province. Although it declined after the late Heian period, it was revived by the [[Ōtomo clan]], from the [[Kamakura period]] onwards. In March 1408, Ōtomo Shinze relocated the shrine from the top of the mountain to its current location at the foot of the mountain. During the [[Edo period]], the [[Makino clan]] and then the [[Naitō clan]] of [[Nobeoka Domain]], frequently sponsored renovation and repairs, and their feudal retainers also donated items such as [[tōro|stone lanterns]].{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} During the [[Meiji period]] era of [[State Shinto]], the shrine was designated as a {{nihongo|National shrine, 2nd rank |国幣中社|[[kokuhei-chūsha]]}} under the [[Modern system of ranked Shinto Shrines]]Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' pp. 125. {{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} ==Mannen-bashi== The {{nihongo|Mannenbashi|万年橋||}} is a 22-meter long single-arch stone bridge that spans the Samuda River (commonly known as the Misogi River), which flows through the entrance to Sasamuta Shrine. It was designated as a Tangible Cultural Property of Ōita Prefecture on April 8, 1980. Not only is the main structure an arch, but the road surface also forms a gentle arc, and the stonework between the road surface and the arch is narrow. In 1862 at the end of the Edo period, the village headman of Samuta village, which was then part of the [[Nobeoka Domain]], started a stone masonry business in Shibakita village, Ono district (currently [[Bungo-ono, Ōita]]), which was part of [[Oka Domain]]. ==Gallery== Sasamuta-jinja torii.JPG|Torii Hongusan.JPG|Mout Hongu Sasamuta-jinja honden.JPG|Honden Sasamuta-jinja kaguraden.JPG|Kagura-den Sasamuta-jinja Mannen-bashi.JPG|Mannen-bashi (P.ICIP) ==See also== *[[List of Shinto shrines]] *[[Ichinomiya]] ==References== * Plutschow, Herbe. ''Matsuri: The Festivals of Japan''. RoutledgeCurzon (1996) {{ISBN|1-873410-63-8}} * [[Richard Ponsonby-Fane|Ponsonby-Fane]], Richard Arthur Brabazon. (1959). [https://books.google.com/books?id=SLAeAAAAMAAJ&q=The+Imperial+House+of+Japan ''The Imperial House of Japan.''] Kyoto: Ponsonby Memorial Society. [http://www.worldcat.org/wcpa/oclc/194887 OCLC 194887] ==External links== {{commons Category|Sasamuta-jinja}} *[https://sasamuta.com Official home page] The main festival of the shrine is held annually on April 15.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Sasamuta Jinja is {{nihongo|'''Sasamuta-Ōkami'''|西寒多大神|}}, which is an amalgamation of: * {{nihongo|'''[[Amaterasu]]'''|天照皇大御神|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto]]'''|月読尊|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Ame-no-oshihomimi]]'''|天忍穗耳尊|}} ==History== According to the ''Ōita Gunshi'' (大分郡志), [[Empress Jingu]] visited Mount Sasamuta on her way back from the conquest of the [[Korean Peninsula]], and planted a white flag at the top of the mountain as proof of her visit. The local people revered it and tied a fence around it to worship it. Later, in April of the 9th year of [[Emperor Ojin]]'s reign, [[Takenouchi no Sukune]] built a shrine on the site, which established that the mountain was a [[sacred mountain]]. The shrine first appears in documentary history in an article dated March 22, 869, in the ''[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]'', where it is written that Sasamuta-Ōkami was given the rank of Junior Fifth Rank. It reappears in the ''[[Engishiki]]'' listing of the mid-[[Heian period]], where it has the distinction of being classed as the only "major shrine" in Bungo Province. Although it declined after the late Heian period, it was revived by the [[Ōtomo clan]], from the [[Kamakura period]] onwards. In March 1408, Ōtomo Shinze relocated the shrine from the top of the mountain to its current location at the foot of the mountain. During the [[Edo period]], the [[Makino clan]] and then the [[Naitō clan]] of [[Nobeoka Domain]], frequently sponsored renovation and repairs, and their feudal retainers also donated items such as [[tōro|stone lanterns]].{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} During the [[Meiji period]] era of [[State Shinto]], the shrine was designated as a {{nihongo|National shrine, 2nd rank |国幣中社|[[kokuhei-chūsha]]}} under the [[Modern system of ranked Shinto Shrines]]Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' pp. 125. {{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} ==Mannen-bashi== The {{nihongo|Mannenbashi|万年橋||}} is a 22-meter long single-arch stone bridge that spans the Samuda River (commonly known as the Misogi River), which flows through the entrance to Sasamuta Shrine. It was designated as a Tangible Cultural Property of Ōita Prefecture on April 8, 1980. Not only is the main structure an arch, but the road surface also forms a gentle arc, and the stonework between the road surface and the arch is narrow. In 1862 at the end of the Edo period, the village headman of Samuta village, which was then part of the [[Nobeoka Domain]], started a stone masonry business in Shibakita village, Ono district (currently [[Bungo-ono, Ōita]]), which was part of [[Oka Domain]]. ==Gallery== Sasamuta-jinja torii.JPG|Torii Hongusan.JPG|Mout Hongu Sasamuta-jinja honden.JPG|Honden Sasamuta-jinja kaguraden.JPG|Kagura-den Sasamuta-jinja Mannen-bashi.JPG|Mannen-bashi (P.ICIP) ==See also== *[[List of Shinto shrines]] *[[Ichinomiya]] ==References== * Plutschow, Herbe. 西寒多神社 | image = Sasamuta-jinja haiden-2.JPG | caption = Haiden of Sasamuta Jinja {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Oita Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|33|10|22|N|131|35|54.2|E|region:JP-35|display=inline,title}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = | deity = Sasamuta-Ōkami | founded_by = | established = unknown | date_destroyed = | location = 1644 Soda, Ōita-shi, Ōita-ken | website = | architecture_style = | festival =April 15 | leadership = | footnotes = }} {{nihongo|'''Sasamuta Jinja'''|西寒多神社}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in the Soda neighborhood of the city of [[Ōita, Ōita | Ōita]] in [[Ōita Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is one of the shrines claiming to be the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of former [[Bungo Province]]. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on April 15.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Sasamuta Jinja is {{nihongo|'''Sasamuta-Ōkami'''|西寒多大神|}}, which is an amalgamation of: * {{nihongo|'''[[Amaterasu]]'''|天照皇大御神|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto]]'''|月読尊|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Ame-no-oshihomimi]]'''|天忍穗耳尊|}} ==History== According to the ''Ōita Gunshi'' (大分郡志), [[Empress Jingu]] visited Mount Sasamuta on her way back from the conquest of the [[Korean Peninsula]], and planted a white flag at the top of the mountain as proof of her visit. The local people revered it and tied a fence around it to worship it. Later, in April of the 9th year of [[Emperor Ojin]]'s reign, [[Takenouchi no Sukune]] built a shrine on the site, which established that the mountain was a [[sacred mountain]]. The shrine first appears in documentary history in an article dated March 22, 869, in the ''[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]'', where it is written that Sasamuta-Ōkami was given the rank of Junior Fifth Rank. It reappears in the ''[[Engishiki]]'' listing of the mid-[[Heian period]], where it has the distinction of being classed as the only "major shrine" in Bungo Province. Although it declined after the late Heian period, it was revived by the [[Ōtomo clan]], from the [[Kamakura period]] onwards. In March 1408, Ōtomo Shinze relocated the shrine from the top of the mountain to its current location at the foot of the mountain. During the [[Edo period]], the [[Makino clan]] and then the [[Naitō clan]] of [[Nobeoka Domain]], frequently sponsored renovation and repairs, and their feudal retainers also donated items such as [[tōro|stone lanterns]].{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} During the [[Meiji period]] era of [[State Shinto]], the shrine was designated as a {{nihongo|National shrine, 2nd rank |国幣中社|[[kokuhei-chūsha]]}} under the [[Modern system of ranked Shinto Shrines]]Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' pp. 125. {{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} ==Mannen-bashi== The {{nihongo|Mannenbashi|万年橋||}} is a 22-meter long single-arch stone bridge that spans the Samuda River (commonly known as the Misogi River), which flows through the entrance to Sasamuta Shrine. It was designated as a Tangible Cultural Property of Ōita Prefecture on April 8, 1980. Not only is the main structure an arch, but the road surface also forms a gentle arc, and the stonework between the road surface and the arch is narrow. In 1862 at the end of the Edo period, the village headman of Samuta village, which was then part of the [[Nobeoka Domain]], started a stone masonry business in Shibakita village, Ono district (currently [[Bungo-ono, Ōita]]), which was part of [[Oka Domain]]. ==Gallery== Sasamuta-jinja torii.JPG|Torii Hongusan.JPG|Mout Hongu Sasamuta-jinja honden.JPG|Honden Sasamuta-jinja kaguraden.JPG|Kagura-den Sasamuta-jinja Mannen-bashi.JPG|Mannen-bashi (P.ICIP) ==See also== *[[List of Shinto shrines]] *[[Ichinomiya]] ==References== * Plutschow, Herbe. ''Matsuri: The Festivals of Japan''. RoutledgeCurzon (1996) {{ISBN|1-873410-63-8}} * [[Richard Ponsonby-Fane|Ponsonby-Fane]], Richard Arthur Brabazon. (1959). [https://books.google.com/books?id=SLAeAAAAMAAJ&q=The+Imperial+House+of+Japan ''The Imperial House of Japan.''] Kyoto: Ponsonby Memorial Society. [http://www.worldcat.org/wcpa/oclc/194887 OCLC 194887] ==External links== {{commons Category|Sasamuta-jinja}} *[https://sasamuta.com Official home page] *[https://www.hyogo-jinjacho.com/data/6323031.html Hyogo Jinjacho home page] ==Notes== {{reflist}} {{Shinto shrine}} {{Munakata Faith}} {{Beppyo Shrines}} {{Ichinomiya}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Pages that used to use Authority control]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Ōita Prefecture]] [[Category:Bungo Province]] [[Category: Ōita (city)]] [[Category:Ichinomiya]] [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:11]] [[Category:Shikinai Taisha]] [[Category:Kokuhei Chūsha]] [[Category:Oita Prefecture designated tangible cultural property]] [[Category:Pages and Categories from Wikipedia 4]] [[Category:11 4]] [[Category:mm]] [[Category:Sasamuta Shrine]] [[Category:bump 1-26]] [[Category:Munakata Faith]] [[Category:New]] [[Category:C111]] [[Category:Pages and Categories from Wikipedia]] }} [[en:Sasamuta Shrine]] [[sn:Sasamuta Shrine]]

{{Short description|Shinto shrine in Ōita Prefecture, Japan}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Sasamuta Jinja
西寒多神社 | image = Sasamuta-jinja haiden-2.JPG | caption = Haiden of Sasamuta Jinja {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Oita Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|33|10|22|N|131|35|54.2|E|region:JP-35|display=inline,title}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = | deity = Sasamuta-Ōkami | founded_by = | established = unknown | date_destroyed = | location = 1644 Soda, Ōita-shi, Ōita-ken | website = | architecture_style = | festival =April 15 | leadership = | footnotes = }} {{nihongo|'''Sasamuta Jinja'''|西寒多神社}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in the Soda neighborhood of the city of [[Ōita, Ōita | Ōita]] in [[Ōita Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is one of the shrines claiming to be the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of former [[Bungo Province]]. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on April 15.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Sasamuta Jinja is {{nihongo|'''Sasamuta-Ōkami'''|西寒多大神|}}, which is an amalgamation of: * {{nihongo|'''[[Amaterasu]]'''|天照皇大御神|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto]]'''|月読尊|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Ame-no-oshihomimi]]'''|天忍穗耳尊|}} ==History== According to the ''Ōita Gunshi'' (大分郡志), [[Empress Jingu]] visited Mount Sasamuta on her way back from the conquest of the [[Korean Peninsula]], and planted a white flag at the top of the mountain as proof of her visit. The local people revered it and tied a fence around it to worship it. Later, in April of the 9th year of [[Emperor Ojin]]'s reign, [[Takenouchi no Sukune]] built a shrine on the site, which established that the mountain was a [[sacred mountain]]. The shrine first appears in documentary history in an article dated March 22, 869, in the ''[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]'', where it is written that Sasamuta-Ōkami was given the rank of Junior Fifth Rank. It reappears in the ''[[Engishiki]]'' listing of the mid-[[Heian period]], where it has the distinction of being classed as the only "major shrine" in Bungo Province. Although it declined after the late Heian period, it was revived by the [[Ōtomo clan]], from the [[Kamakura period]] onwards. In March 1408, Ōtomo Shinze relocated the shrine from the top of the mountain to its current location at the foot of the mountain. During the [[Edo period]], the [[Makino clan]] and then the [[Naitō clan]] of [[Nobeoka Domain]], frequently sponsored renovation and repairs, and their feudal retainers also donated items such as [[tōro|stone lanterns]].{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} During the [[Meiji period]] era of [[State Shinto]], the shrine was designated as a {{nihongo|National shrine, 2nd rank |国幣中社|[[kokuhei-chūsha]]}} under the [[Modern system of ranked Shinto Shrines]]Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' pp. 125. {{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} ==Mannen-bashi== The {{nihongo|Mannenbashi|万年橋||}} is a 22-meter long single-arch stone bridge that spans the Samuda River (commonly known as the Misogi River), which flows through the entrance to Sasamuta Shrine. It was designated as a Tangible Cultural Property of Ōita Prefecture on April 8, 1980. Not only is the main structure an arch, but the road surface also forms a gentle arc, and the stonework between the road surface and the arch is narrow. In 1862 at the end of the Edo period, the village headman of Samuta village, which was then part of the [[Nobeoka Domain]], started a stone masonry business in Shibakita village, Ono district (currently [[Bungo-ono, Ōita]]), which was part of [[Oka Domain]]. ==Gallery== Sasamuta-jinja torii.JPG|Torii Hongusan.JPG|Mout Hongu Sasamuta-jinja honden.JPG|Honden Sasamuta-jinja kaguraden.JPG|Kagura-den Sasamuta-jinja Mannen-bashi.JPG|Mannen-bashi (P.ICIP) ==See also== *[[List of Shinto shrines]] *[[Ichinomiya]] ==References== * Plutschow, Herbe. ''Matsuri: The Festivals of Japan''. RoutledgeCurzon (1996) {{ISBN|1-873410-63-8}} * [[Richard Ponsonby-Fane|Ponsonby-Fane]], Richard Arthur Brabazon. (1959). [https://books.google.com/books?id=SLAeAAAAMAAJ&q=The+Imperial+House+of+Japan ''The Imperial House of Japan.''] Kyoto: Ponsonby Memorial Society. [http://www.worldcat.org/wcpa/oclc/194887 OCLC 194887] ==External links== {{commons Category|Sasamuta-jinja}} *[https://sasamuta.com Official home page] *[https://www.hyogo-jinjacho.com/data/6323031.html Hyogo Jinjacho home page] ==Notes== {{reflist}} {{Shinto shrine}} {{Munakata Faith}} {{Beppyo Shrines}} {{Ichinomiya}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Pages that used to use Authority control]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Ōita Prefecture]] [[Category:Bungo Province]] [[Category: Ōita (city)]] [[Category:Ichinomiya]] [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:11]] [[Category:Shikinai Taisha]] [[Category:Kokuhei Chūsha]] [[Category:Oita Prefecture designated tangible cultural property]] [[Category:Pages and Categories from Wikipedia 4]] [[Category:11 4]] [[Category:mm]] [[Category:Sasamuta Shrine]] [[Category:Munakata Faith]] [[Category:New]] [[Category:Pages and Categories from Wikipedia]] [[Category:qq]][[sn:Sasamuta Shrine]][[Category:qq]] }} [[en:Sasamuta Shrine]] [[sn:Sasamuta Shrine]]

The main festival of the shrine is held annually on April 15.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Sasamuta Jinja is {{nihongo|'''Sasamuta-Ōkami'''|西寒多大神|}}, which is an amalgamation of: * {{nihongo|'''[[Amaterasu]]'''|天照皇大御神|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto]]'''|月読尊|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Ame-no-oshihomimi]]'''|天忍穗耳尊|}} ==History== According to the ''Ōita Gunshi'' (大分郡志), [[Empress Jingu]] visited Mount Sasamuta on her way back from the conquest of the [[Korean Peninsula]], and planted a white flag at the top of the mountain as proof of her visit. The local people revered it and tied a fence around it to worship it. Later, in April of the 9th year of [[Emperor Ojin]]'s reign, [[Takenouchi no Sukune]] built a shrine on the site, which established that the mountain was a [[sacred mountain]]. The shrine first appears in documentary history in an article dated March 22, 869, in the ''[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]'', where it is written that Sasamuta-Ōkami was given the rank of Junior Fifth Rank. It reappears in the ''[[Engishiki]]'' listing of the mid-[[Heian period]], where it has the distinction of being classed as the only "major shrine" in Bungo Province. Although it declined after the late Heian period, it was revived by the [[Ōtomo clan]], from the [[Kamakura period]] onwards. In March 1408, Ōtomo Shinze relocated the shrine from the top of the mountain to its current location at the foot of the mountain. During the [[Edo period]], the [[Makino clan]] and then the [[Naitō clan]] of [[Nobeoka Domain]], frequently sponsored renovation and repairs, and their feudal retainers also donated items such as [[tōro|stone lanterns]].{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} During the [[Meiji period]] era of [[State Shinto]], the shrine was designated as a {{nihongo|National shrine, 2nd rank |国幣中社|[[kokuhei-chūsha]]}} under the [[Modern system of ranked Shinto Shrines]]Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' pp. 125. {{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} ==Mannen-bashi== The {{nihongo|Mannenbashi|万年橋||}} is a 22-meter long single-arch stone bridge that spans the Samuda River (commonly known as the Misogi River), which flows through the entrance to Sasamuta Shrine. It was designated as a Tangible Cultural Property of Ōita Prefecture on April 8, 1980. Not only is the main structure an arch, but the road surface also forms a gentle arc, and the stonework between the road surface and the arch is narrow. In 1862 at the end of the Edo period, the village headman of Samuta village, which was then part of the [[Nobeoka Domain]], started a stone masonry business in Shibakita village, Ono district (currently [[Bungo-ono, Ōita]]), which was part of [[Oka Domain]]. ==Gallery== Sasamuta-jinja torii.JPG|Torii Hongusan.JPG|Mout Hongu Sasamuta-jinja honden.JPG|Honden Sasamuta-jinja kaguraden.JPG|Kagura-den Sasamuta-jinja Mannen-bashi.JPG|Mannen-bashi (P.ICIP) ==See also== *[[List of Shinto shrines]] *[[Ichinomiya]] ==References== * Plutschow, Herbe. Later, in April of the 9th year of [[Emperor Ojin]]'s reign, [[Takenouchi no Sukune]] built a shrine on the site, which established that the mountain was a [[sacred mountain]]. The shrine first appears in documentary history in an article dated March 22, 869, in the ''[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]'', where it is written that Sasamuta-Ōkami was given the Rank of Junior Fifth Rank. It reappears in the ''[[Engishiki]]'' listing of the mid-[[Heian period]], where it has the distinction of being classed as the only "major shrine" in Bungo Province. Although it declined after the late Heian period, it was revived by the [[Ōtomo clan]], from the [[Kamakura period]] onwards. In March 1408, Ōtomo Shinze relocated the shrine from the top of the mountain to its current location at the foot of the mountain. During the [[Edo period]], the [[Makino clan]] and then the [[Naitō clan]] of [[Nobeoka Domain]], frequently sponsored renovation and repairs, and their feudal retainers also donated items such as [[tōro|stone lanterns]].{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} During the [[Meiji period]] era of [[State Shinto]], the shrine was designated as a {{nihongo|National shrine, 2nd Rank |国幣中社|[[kokuhei-chūsha]]}} under the [[Modern system of Ranked Shinto Shrines]]Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' pp. 125. {{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} ==Mannen-bashi== The {{nihongo|Mannenbashi|万年橋||}} is a 22-meter long single-arch stone bridge that spans the Samuda River (commonly known as the Misogi River), which flows through the entrance to Sasamuta Shrine. It was designated as a Tangible Cultural Property of Ōita Prefecture on April 8, 1980. Not only is the main structure an arch, but the road surface also forms a gentle arc, and the stonework between the road surface and the arch is narrow. It is one of the shrines claiming to be the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of former [[Bungo Province]]. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on April 15.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Sasamuta Jinja is {{nihongo|'''Sasamuta-Ōkami'''|西寒多大神|}}, which is an amalgamation of: * {{nihongo|'''[[Amaterasu]]'''|天照皇大御神|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto]]'''|月読尊|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[:en:Ame-no-oshihomimi|Ame-no-oshihomimi]]'''|天忍穗耳尊|}} ==History== According to the ''Ōita Gunshi'' (大分郡志), [[Empress Jingu]] visited Mount Sasamuta on her way back from the conquest of the [[Korean Peninsula]], and planted a white flag at the top of the mountain as proof of her visit. The local people revered it and tied a fence around it to worship it. Later, in April of the 9th year of [[Emperor Ojin]]'s reign, [[Takenouchi no Sukune]] built a shrine on the site, which established that the mountain was a [[sacred mountain]]. The shrine first appears in documentary history in an article dated March 22, 869, in the ''[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]'', where it is written that Sasamuta-Ōkami was given the Rank of Junior Fifth Rank. It reappears in the ''[[Engishiki]]'' listing of the mid-[[Heian period]], where it has the distinction of being classed as the only "major shrine" in Bungo Province. Although it declined after the late Heian period, it was revived by the [[Ōtomo clan]], from the [[Kamakura period]] onwards. In March 1408, Ōtomo Shinze relocated the shrine from the top of the mountain to its current location at the foot of the mountain. During the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]], the [[Makino clan]] and then the [[Naitō clan]] of [[Nobeoka Domain]], frequently sponsored renovation and repairs, and their feudal retainers also donated items such as [[tōro|stone lanterns]].{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} During the [[Meiji period]] era of [[State Shinto]], the shrine was designated as a {{nihongo|National shrine, 2nd Rank |国幣中社|[[kokuhei-chūsha]]}} under the [[Modern system of Ranked Shinto Shrines]]Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' pp. 125. {{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} ==Mannen-bashi== The {{nihongo|Mannenbashi|万年橋||}} is a 22-meter long single-arch stone bridge that spans the Samuda River (commonly known as the Misogi River), which flows through the entrance to Sasamuta Shrine. It is one of the shrines claiming to be the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of former [[Bungo Province]]. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on April 15.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Sasamuta Jinja is {{nihongo|'''Sasamuta-Ōkami'''|西寒多大神|}}, which is an amalgamation of: * {{nihongo|'''[[Amaterasu]]'''|天照皇大御神|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto]]'''|月読尊|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[:en:Ame-no-oshihomimi|Ame-no-oshihomimi]]'''|天忍穗耳尊|}} ==History== According to the ''Ōita Gunshi'' (大分郡志), [[Empress Jingu]] visited Mount Sasamuta on her way back from the conquest of the [[Korean Peninsula]], and planted a white flag at the top of the mountain as proof of her visit. The local people revered it and tied a fence around it to worship it. Later, in April of the 9th year of [[:en:Emperor Ojin|Emperor Ojin]]'s reign, [[Takenouchi no Sukune]] built a shrine on the site, which established that the mountain was a [[sacred mountain]]. The shrine first appears in documentary history in an article dated March 22, 869, in the ''[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]'', where it is written that Sasamuta-Ōkami was given the Rank of Junior Fifth Rank. It reappears in the ''[[Engishiki]]'' listing of the mid-[[Heian period]], where it has the distinction of being classed as the only "major shrine" in Bungo Province. Although it declined after the late Heian period, it was revived by the [[:en:Ōtomo clan|Ōtomo clan]], from the [[Kamakura period]] onwards. In March 1408, Ōtomo Shinze relocated the shrine from the top of the mountain to its current location at the foot of the mountain. During the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]], the [[Makino clan]] and then the [[Naitō clan]] of [[Nobeoka Domain]], frequently sponsored renovation and repairs, and their feudal retainers also donated items such as [[tōro|stone lanterns]].{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} During the [[Meiji period]] era of [[State Shinto]], the shrine was designated as a {{nihongo|National shrine, 2nd Rank |国幣中社|[[kokuhei-chūsha]]}} under the [[Modern system of Ranked Shinto Shrines]]Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' pp. 125. {{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} ==Mannen-bashi== The {{nihongo|Mannenbashi|万年橋||}} is a 22-meter long single-arch stone bridge that spans the Samuda River (commonly known as the Misogi River), which flows through the entrance to Sasamuta Shrine. It was designated as a Tangible Cultural Property of Ōita Prefecture on April 8, 1980. Not only is the main structure an arch, but the road surface also forms a gentle arc, and the stonework between the road surface and the arch is narrow. It is one of the shrines claiming to be the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of former [[:en:Bungo Province|Bungo Province]]. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on April 15.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Sasamuta Jinja is {{nihongo|'''Sasamuta-Ōkami'''|西寒多大神|}}, which is an amalgamation of: * {{nihongo|'''[[Amaterasu]]'''|天照皇大御神|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto]]'''|月読尊|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[:en:Ame-no-oshihomimi|Ame-no-oshihomimi]]'''|天忍穗耳尊|}} ==History== According to the ''Ōita Gunshi'' (大分郡志), [[:en:Empress Jingū|Empress Jingū]] visited Mount Sasamuta on her way back from the conquest of the [[Korean Peninsula]], and planted a white flag at the top of the mountain as proof of her visit. The local people revered it and tied a fence around it to worship it. Later, in April of the 9th year of [[:en:Emperor Ojin|Emperor Ojin]]'s reign, [[Takenouchi no Sukune]] built a shrine on the site, which established that the mountain was a [[sacred mountain]]. The shrine first appears in documentary history in an article dated March 22, 869, in the ''[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]'', where it is written that Sasamuta-Ōkami was given the Rank of Junior Fifth Rank. It reappears in the ''[[Engishiki]]'' listing of the mid-[[:en:Heian period|Heian period]], where it has the distinction of being classed as the only "major shrine" in Bungo Province. Although it declined after the late Heian period, it was revived by the [[:en:Ōtomo clan|Ōtomo clan]], from the [[Kamakura period]] onwards. In March 1408, Ōtomo Shinze relocated the shrine from the top of the mountain to its current location at the foot of the mountain. During the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]], the [[Makino clan]] and then the [[Naitō clan]] of [[Nobeoka Domain]], frequently sponsored renovation and repairs, and their feudal retainers also donated items such as [[tōro|stone lanterns]].{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} During the [[Meiji period]] era of [[State Shinto]], the shrine was designated as a {{nihongo|National shrine, 2nd Rank |国幣中社|[[kokuhei-chūsha]]}} under the [[Modern system of Ranked Shinto Shrines]]Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' pp. 125. {{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} ==Mannen-bashi== The {{nihongo|Mannenbashi|万年橋||}} is a 22-meter long single-arch stone bridge that spans the Samuda River (commonly known as the Misogi River), which flows through the entrance to Sasamuta Shrine. It was designated as a Tangible Cultural Property of Ōita Prefecture on April 8, 1980. Not only is the main structure an arch, but the road surface also forms a gentle arc, and the stonework between the road surface and the arch is narrow. In 1862 at the end of the Edo period, the village headman of Samuta village, which was then part of the [[Nobeoka Domain]], started a stone masonry business in Shibakita village, Ono district (currently [[:en:Bungo-ono, Ōita|Bungo-ono, Ōita]]), which was part of [[Oka Domain]]. ==Gallery== Sasamuta-jinja torii.JPG|Torii Hongusan.JPG|Mout Hongu Sasamuta-jinja honden.JPG|Honden Sasamuta-jinja kaguraden.JPG|Kagura-den Sasamuta-jinja Mannen-bashi.JPG|Mannen-bashi (P.ICIP) ==See also== *[[List of Shinto shrines]] *[[Ichinomiya]] ==References== * Plutschow, Herbe. It is one of the shrines claiming to be the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of former [[:en:Bungo Province|Bungo Province]]. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on April 15.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Sasamuta Jinja is {{nihongo|'''Sasamuta-Ōkami'''|西寒多大神|}}, which is an amalgamation of: * {{nihongo|'''[[Amaterasu]]'''|天照皇大御神|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto]]'''|月読尊|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[:en:Ame-no-oshihomimi|Ame-no-oshihomimi]]'''|天忍穗耳尊|}} ==History== According to the ''Ōita Gunshi'' (大分郡志), [[:en:Empress Jingū|Empress Jingū]] visited Mount Sasamuta on her way back from the conquest of the [[:en:Korea|Korea]], and planted a white flag at the top of the mountain as proof of her visit. The local people revered it and tied a fence around it to worship it. Later, in April of the 9th year of [[:en:Emperor Ojin|Emperor Ojin]]'s reign, [[Takenouchi no Sukune]] built a shrine on the site, which established that the mountain was a [[sacred mountain]]. The shrine first appears in documentary history in an article dated March 22, 869, in the ''[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]'', where it is written that Sasamuta-Ōkami was given the Rank of Junior Fifth Rank. It reappears in the ''[[Engishiki]]'' listing of the mid-[[:en:Heian period|Heian period]], where it has the distinction of being classed as the only "major shrine" in Bungo Province. Although it declined after the late Heian period, it was revived by the [[:en:Ōtomo clan|Ōtomo clan]], from the [[:en:Kamakura period|Kamakura period]] onwards. In March 1408, Ōtomo Shinze relocated the shrine from the top of the mountain to its current location at the foot of the mountain. During the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]], the [[:en:Makino clan|Makino clan]] and then the [[Naitō clan]] of [[Nobeoka Domain]], frequently sponsored renovation and repairs, and their feudal retainers also donated items such as [[tōro|stone lanterns]].{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} During the [[Meiji period]] era of [[:en:State Shinto|State Shinto]], the shrine was designated as a {{nihongo|National shrine, 2nd Rank |国幣中社|[[:en:Kokuhei-chūsha|Kokuhei-chūsha]]}} under the [[Modern system of Ranked Shinto Shrines]]Ponsonby-Fane, Richard.
